description: Every dataset tells a story, but not every story is true. We're a crew of coders, designers and data nerds who treat NASA's Earth data like a crime scene: question everything, trust the evidence, ignore the noise. In one weekend we'll turn raw satellite records into something anyone can investigate. Our toolkit: Python, ML, web dev, design, video and stubborn statistics. Our rule: if the data can't prove it, we don't claim it.
summary:
Noise Trap answers one question about Earth data: is this trend real, or just noise? The usual trend test (Mann-Kendall) treats every month as independent, but climate data is "sticky": a warm month tends to follow a warm month. That makes the usual test far too confident. On simulated data with no trend at all, it reports a trend 32% of the time instead of 5%.

Noise Trap runs three stages side by side on NASA data: the usual test, the same test with the stickiness removed (pre-whitening), and an honest verdict that also controls false discoveries when many places are tested at once. A global atlas of 2,016 NASA POWER points shows the gap: the usual test says root-zone soil wetness changed at 71% of land points, but only 19% hold up.

For any place, region, season or headline, the app follows the challenge's five steps and answers in plain words. It gives a rate per decade and a 95% range. When a trend is not proven yet, it says an estimate of how many additional years of observations may be needed to detect the trend, assuming the current trend rate and noise characteristics continue. The core app works offline.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Noise Trap checks whether a trend in NASA Earth data is real or just noise, and shows side by side how the standard test gets it wrong.

The problem: the usual trend test (Mann-Kendall) assumes each month is independent. Climate data is not. A warm month is usually followed by another warm month, and wet soil stays wet. This "stickiness" (autocorrelation) makes the usual test far too confident. On simulated data with no trend at all, it reports a trend 32% of the time, where it should be 5%.

HOW IT WORKS: THREE STAGES, ALWAYS SHOWN TOGETHER

1. Usual test: plain Mann-Kendall, kept on purpose so users can see where it goes wrong.

2. Stickiness removed: lag-1 pre-whitening (Kulkarni & von Storch 1995). We chose it by simulation over six competing corrections. It was the only one near 5% false alarms at every level of stickiness.

3. Honest verdict: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control (q = 0.10) whenever many places, seasons or variables are tested at once (Wilks 2016).

Every answer is in plain words: "trend is real", "not proven yet", "the data point the other way". It comes with Sen's slope per decade and a 95% range. When a trend is not proven, it also gives how many more years of data would settle it (Weatherhead et al. 1998). Noise Trap says whether something changed, never why.

THE CHALLENGE'S FIVE STEPS

1. Choose a variable: 19 NASA POWER variables. Users who don't know the names answer three plain questions and get suggested variables, each with a one-line definition.

2. Choose a region: any point on a world map, nine preset regions, or the whole-globe atlas.

3. Choose a time frame: 1981-2025, any sub-period, any season.

4. Build the time series: the monthly NASA record with seasons removed. Missing months stay missing and are never filled in.

5. Test significance: the three stages above, plus the years still needed.

FEATURES

- Global Trend Atlas: an interactive globe of 2,016 sample points and 5 variables. Switch from the usual test to the honest verdict and watch the false alarms disappear. Extra layers show when each trend will be provable, which places have left their old normal (signal-to-noise, simplified from Hawkins & Sutton 2012, with categories from Frame et al. 2017), and compound change such as hotter and drier at the same point.

- The trap: pure noise with a stickiness slider. The usual test invents trends; the honest one stays clean.

- Investigate one place, scan a region, and case files, including a satellite case: summer haze over Wisconsin from MODIS on Aqua, +0.071 per decade, honest p = 0.023.

- Check a headline: paste a claim such as "Chennai is getting hotter" and get a verdict.

- Second witness: A satellite-derived record and a model-based reanalysis record are analysed separately to examine whether their observed trends agree. Their limitations and potential data dependencies are acknowledged.

- Train your eye: a ten-round game. Guess "real trend" or "just noise", then see what both tests said. A class can share a seed so everyone gets the same ten rounds.

- AI Detective: ask in plain English. The AI calls our statistics tools, and every number in its answer is checked against the tool output.

- MCP connector: other AI apps can call the same 10 tools.

RESULTS ON REAL NASA DATA

Strong signals barely move: air temperature is flagged at 87% of points by the usual test and 79% by the honest verdict. Sticky signals collapse: soil wetness goes from 71% to 19%. We are not claiming nothing changes. We show which changes the data can prove.

Chennai warming: the usual test gives p = 0.0027, which looks certain. The honest answer is p = 0.054: not proven yet.

VALIDATION (where the true answer is known)

- False alarms on sticky noise (phi = 0.6, should be 5%): usual test 32.0%, Noise Trap 3.8%.

- A 30x30 map of pure noise: usual test flags 15.6% of pixels, Noise Trap 0.0%.

- A real trend planted in half a map: about 1 in 15 of Noise Trap's flags are false (target: under 1 in 10).

- The 95% range contains the true rate 93-98% of the time, even with 30% of months missing.

- Our Mann-Kendall matches the reference library pymannkendall to 1e-10. 153 backend tests and 5 frontend tests cover the statistics and every published data file.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students, journalists, teachers and the public see trend charts every day but have no way to tell a real change from a run of random wiggles. Noise Trap gives a clear verdict in plain language, shows the evidence behind it, and says honestly when the data cannot answer yet. That protects people from both false alarms and false reassurance.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, pymannkendall, FastAPI) for the statistics and API; JavaScript with React, Vite, Plotly.js and d3-geo for the web app. Hosted on Vercel (web) and Render (API). There is no database: every result is a static JSON file anyone can open, and most of the app works with no server at all.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most trend tools show only one answer. Noise Trap shows the wrong answer next to the right one, so people learn why the usual test fails instead of just trusting a new number. The globe animation, the trap simulator and the Train your eye game make a statistical idea something you can see and play with.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Honest labelling: NASA POWER is based on the MERRA-2 reanalysis, a model, and is labelled as a model everywhere. Satellite records are labelled as satellite.

- Worldview images are shown as illustrations only; the charts are the evidence.

- No causal claims: the app says whether something changed, never why.

- Accessibility: a colour-blind-safe palette (orange = usual test, blue = honest verdict), keyboard controls and plain language.

- Security: API keys stay on the server, and live AI questions need a passcode so a public link cannot use up the key.

LIMITS (also stated in the app)

Simulations model one-month memory (AR(1)) only. Only straight-line (monotonic) trends are tested. With very sticky data (phi 0.8 or more), the honest test needs a longer record. MERRA-2 is a reanalysis model, not a direct observation.

USE OF AI TOOLS

We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code) for coding, debugging, research, writing and UI design. Every statistic in the app is computed by our own tested code, not by an AI. Inside the app, Google Gemini powers the AI Detective and Check a headline; it calls our statistics tools, and its numbers are checked against the tool output.
